summary: This program asks the builder for a house's address, bedroom and bathroom counts, and then for a list of rooms with their use and dimensions. It stores each room as a Room object inside a House object and prints the finished layout back out.

lines.text: ArrayList is the resizable list implementation used to collect the rooms as they are entered, since the number of rooms is not known until the builder types it in.
A Scanner wrapped around System.in is how the program reads whatever the builder types at the keyboard.
nextLine reads the whole line, so an address with spaces in it stays in one piece.
Bathrooms are a double rather than an int because half baths are normal in a floor plan.
This count controls how many times the room-entry loop will run.
After reading a number, the newline the builder pressed is still waiting in the scanner; this extra nextLine throws it away so the next nextLine does not come back empty.
The variable is declared as the List interface but created as an ArrayList, which is the usual Java habit of programming to the more general type.
Counting from 1 up to roomCount makes the prompts read naturally as "room 1", "room 2", and so on.
Each pass through the loop packages the three answers into one Room object and appends it to the list, so related values travel together instead of in three parallel lists.

lines.code: House house = new House(address, bedrooms, bathrooms);
lines.text: The House constructor takes the facts that describe the property as a whole.
The layout is attached afterwards with a setter, because the rooms could not be collected until the house's basic details were known.
Passing the whole House object to one method keeps main short and gives the printing logic a single job.
This helper is private because nothing outside HouseBuilder needs it, and static because it is called from main without an instance.
Asking the list for its size reports the real number of rooms stored, rather than trusting the count the builder typed.
The enhanced for loop visits each Room in turn without any index bookkeeping.
Each Room is asked for its own data through its getters, which is the object doing the work of describing itself.
